utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Tom Kuzmanovic here for Colonel Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Vesna Alaburic attorney, and I'm Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Accused Valentin Coric, Tomislav Jonjic, attorney-at-law in Zagreb, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Defence of Mr. Pusic, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, my name is Slobodan Praljak and I represent myself, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me greet all those people present here. I'd like to greet the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm glad to see that one of them is a French-speaking lawyer. I'd like to greet the counsels for the Defence. I'd like to greet Mr. Praljak as well and let me not forget greet the interpret test who are assisting us as well as all the personnel of the Trial Chamber, the Registrar and all the other assistants. As you know, this is a Pre-Trial Conference. I've sent an agenda to you in advance and I'm going to slightly amend the agenda because this morning, I was advised of a new motion filed by the Prosecution following an order filed on the 24th of January 2006. There are a number of problems, a number of issues that prevent -- that are preventing the trial from being ready for trial. The first issue, the first problem, has to do with Mr. Praljak and with the fact that he is representing himself. As you are well aware, Mr. Praljak has filed a motion with the Chamber for counsel to be assigned to him. I immediately asked the Prosecution as well as various Defence counsels, I asked them to give me their own opinion, their own position, about the merits of the motion. Various pleadings were filed in response and thus the Trial Chamber will very soon be in a position to make a decision. And that's the reason why I will meet the two other judges of Trial Chamber II in order for us to establish our position following the motion filed by Mr. Praljak. In order to give enough information to the -- my fellow judges tomorrow, I will list a number of issues that are relevant in this case and I will later on ask Mr. Praljak for any comments he might have about the situation. As I've already stated before, according to the Statute of the Tribunal, accused is perfectly entitled to represent himself. It's an absolute right and accused persons have the right to say they want to defend themselves or they want to benefit from the assistance of a lawyer. Funny enough, this Tribunal, in at least two cases I've quoted before in the Milosevic and in the Seselj case, although these two accused did not want to have counsel, their respective Trial Chambers imposed a lawyer upon them without wondering about the financial situation of both these Accused. In this specific case, we are in a completely different situation. We are dealing with an Accused who, in the beginning, had counsel and who then later found himself apparently in a position such that he was not able to pay his lawyer and following that, he informed the Registry that he was not in a position to remunerate his counsel, and then he asked for counsel to be assigned to him. According to the procedure, based both on the Statute and on a directive as well as on the Rules, the Registrar requested from Mr. Praljak that he submit all elements relevant to his financial status. In this specific case, the burden of proof relies on the applicant and not on the Registrar. And in a number of countries, France, United States, Germany and either, when an accused is indigent, it is up to the accused to prove so, it is up to the accused to justify that he is indeed without any financial means and, in that case, counsel is assigned to him, and our Tribunal works that way. Therefore, the Registrar requested from Mr. Praljak any relevant information related to his financial status. Furthermore, the Registrar had information coming from NATO according to which the Accused Praljak had some financial means, had some property. Considering this information and considering the partial responses of Mr. Praljak, the Registrar issued a decision stating that under the Statute, the Registrar was not in a position to assign counsel to Mr. Praljak. This decision was challenged before Trial Chamber I. Trial Chamber I rendered a decision confirming the decision initially taken by the Registrar. In other words, that it is up to the Accused to prove that he is indigent. If we remained at that stage of the discussion then the conclusion would be that Mr. Praljak has to represent himself. As far as I'm concerned, personally I believe that it is not possible because Mr. Praljak is not a lawyer. He has not studied law. He is not a law professor, he's not a lawyer. Therefore, he is unable to file motions and to understand the scope of the trial and to follow in an informed manner all the various stages of the proceedings. I believe that in -- under these circumstances, the conditions necessary to have a fair trial would be endangered. And this leads us to another problem. In this case, we are dealing with six Accused, five Accused who have counsel. If we maintain the system as it is, with Mr. Praljak representing himself, then there would be a very serious risk for the other Accused to be prejudiced by this situation. Thus, that is a factor that should also be taken into account. Third problem, third problem that arose recently. Mr. Praljak does not speak neither English nor French. Mr. Praljak, and that's his right, wants to receive in his language all the filings from the Prosecution. He wants to receive these filings in his language. The pre-trial brief, the list of witnesses, the list of exhibits, as well as any other exhibit written in English and that has not previously been translated into B/C/S. If he does not receive all this -- these exhibits, then the conditions necessary for a fair trial would not be complied with because, as you perfectly well know, in the Statute, it is stated that the Accused needs to be informed in his own language of all of the case against him. And, of course, the case against him is made up of witness statements and Prosecution exhibits. At this stage of the proceedings, I nevertheless take note of the fact that the situation we are faced with currently derives from the attitude of Mr. Praljak who has not fully complied with the repeated requests made by the Registrar about his financial status. From what I was able to understand from the situation, a few years ago, allegedly, Mr. Praljak had shares in a number of companies and he allegedly and directly or indirectly allegedly was the owner of a property. From what I understand from the documents, it seems that some of the property, some of these assets, were given according to procedures I'm not familiar with because none of this is mentioned in these documents. Some of these assets were supposedly given to some of -- members of list family. Today, Mr. Praljak is telling us that he has no means whatsoever, no financial means whatsoever to pay his lawyers and to prepare his defence. As you know, this cost is huge. Let me give you just two examples that come to my mind. The first example relates to a case in Trial Chamber II, the Accused Seselj is requesting from the Registrar the reimbursement of costs incurred in the preparation of his defence for a total of 2.4 million dollars. This is just to give you some idea of the scale of the cost of a defence, and recently I read a press release from Agence France-Presse related to a trial that took place a few years ago, the Blaskic case. It seems that the Croatian government remunerated both Defence counsel in that case for a total of 30 million dollars. Well, when you take that into account you realise that the costs are staggering and in order to be able to face these costs, you have to have enough money to remunerate your counsel, to pay expert witnesses, investigators, et cetera. Mr. Praljak, let me now turn to you, and in order to provide enough information to my fellow judges I'm going to meet tomorrow, I would like to know whether you fully responded to the requests made by the Registrar regarding your financial state of affairs today. What is -- what is it now? Can you give me information about that? Because as you well understand, because of your situation, the proceedings have come to a halt. So I'd like to give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I might take a little more of your time because the discussion between myself and the Registry has been going on for quite sometime. Now all the information that you have received from the Registrar and Registry about the fact that I have not complied with all the requests made of me fully is just not correct. I was duty bound following on from the logics of law and human logics, very precisely, to state what material resources I had at my disposal at the point in time when the indictment was raised against me. So that's a question of principle. And you can put that question in a different way and say it like this: Whether up until the point the indictment was raised whether I was a free man, and if I was a free man, whether, within this freedom was included the right to dispose of my property up to that point in time. Of course, in a manner prescribed by law and on the basis of my own free will, because it was my own property, or whether I should have been deemed to have been guilty previously, in a premeditated way which was not have ranked us among civilised societies but among societies that practised law in the system in which I lived for many years. So that is a question of principle and I would never agree that I did not have the right to dispose of my property as I deemed fit. That is the right I had. Now, outside this question of principle, we can look at the facts. That is to say, what was it that I actually possessed before the indictment was raised? What was this property of mine and what did I have, what did I own at the time the indictment was raised? Now, the burden of proof is on me but it is on me in the way in which I believe this can be proved and shown, and it can be shown and proved in a manner positive, as all other things in law. That is to say to make a precise list of the property I own. Movable, immovable property or any other type of property. And that is what I did. I did this very precisely, together with my counsel at the time. I submitted that information to the Registry. I signed a piece of paper saying that it was the truth, that it was the actual state of affairs, and that I was responsible for writing it materially and before the law. The Registry has the right, of course, to have other information. The Registry has the right not to agree with the facts as I presented them. However, I don't know how I can fulfil the Registry's request proving something which -- of something which I do not known, of not being the owner of some property. On -- in two matters, I overstepped my principles quite a bit and wanted to meet the requests of the Registry. First of all, when I went to the bank, because they had asked me to show that I did not have any bank accounts in that particular bank. Now, apart from that particular bank in Croatia, there are some 70 other banks and so by virtue of negative evidence and proof, they could have asked me to bring in statements from the 70 other banks saying that I don't have any bank accounts in those 70 other banks but this would go against the grain of logic, and negative showing of evidence. Your Honours -- Your Honour, it is very simple. Take it this way. For every company and for any property that they asked me -- my links to, what links I have to them, in a civilised country it is very easy to establish the facts and Croatia is a civilised country today. You can do this in a very clear-cut, legal way, in a very efficacious way, and in a very correct and precise way, and this is the way you would go about it. You could ask the Court or the courts through the organs of the Republic of Croatia or the organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to issue and send in a document stating when the industry in Ljubuski was established, who established it, what capital was used to establish it, and how that basic capital changed and evolved over time, who put in more capital, changed the capital resources of that firm, and so on and so forth. All these are matters which are registered by the Court, and that kind of organisation, and it will provide a clear insight into the matter and you can quite clearly see that no where does my name appear there in those documents. I don't know how you want me by violating the law, go into a research of something with which I have nothing to do, no connection whatsoever. I have already explained that this is something that I do not own, that I am not an investigator of The Hague Tribunal, and that I would have violated the positive laws of both countries if I were to seek information of that kind, which nobody would be duty bound to supply me with in the first place anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: (redacted)I sent them the relative data and information. And it was this: That Mr. -- Dr. Zoran Praljak, that is to say my brother, built that house in 1993. That in 1993, he received a construction permit to build the house. And we have attached that to the documents sent to the registry that in 1994 I think it was he paid money to the city of Zagreb to settle the communal and utilities fees necessary for the construction of the house, and that sometime in the year 2000, I think it was, when the process continued, that same man, Zoran Praljak, continuing the building of the house, asked for the main project and plan for the ground floor level and horticultural surrounding plan, and I'm showing you that document it is the adjudicated facts plan for the ground floor and the surrounding land, and the architectural and construction plan for the sewage system, for the electrical installations and everything else necessary for a plan, and all that was in 2000, as the second stage in the construction of that particular house, and that as I wrote to the Registry, we have several kilograms of documents of the same type as this. Now, I'm asking you why is it -- would it be my duty to investigate my brother for me to prove to you that I am not the owner and proprietor of that house? Furthermore I provided very precise data in evidence showing that my wife brought with her when she married me, a flat that she owned before she married me, before she entered into the marital state with me, and that she allowed me to sell that flat during the war because I needed money, and that this lady with whom I have shared my life for 37 years, we had very good relations as man and wife, I promised her that I would return her flat to her. Now, at the point in time when I had paid for the flat that I have received from the army, when I had paid that out, paid all my dues, I drew up a contract and agreement for a gift, and I signed it in 2002. In March 2002, I returned this flat to her and I also stipulated that if she was ever to leave the marriage, that she could take the flat with her. Now, the discussion I had with the Registry of this Tribunal, Your Honour, imposed upon me the fact that I should have had an additional agreement and contract signed with my wife. Otherwise, the matter would be suspect but I called into question the Registry's right to mirror its culturological models and civilisational models to my own civilisational model and I also questioned the right of the Registry's right to transpose and to superimpose and to place its cultural model and civilisational model above and superior to my own models, because I consider that my oral agreement with my wife is based in the law, it is a fundamental right and a fundamental agreement as would you find in any other country. Therefore, having said that, may I be allowed to continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me sum up your situation or your position in three facets. The first facet is the question of societies. You're telling us that regarding -- or the companies. It was easy to check with the deeds of those companies establishing those companies, it could be shown easily that you were not an owner of any of the three companies. Second aspect, this has to do with your brother's house. You are telling us that initially you had applied for an authorisation to build with your brother, that later on he alone was the one to bear the costs. Third issue, the house you have together with your spouse, and you've just told me that in 2002, you made a gift to her and that you don't deny that, making the gift to her. And the last argument you put forward, and I shall make it known to my colleagues tomorrow, you say that at any rate, whatever may have happened to your personal assets happened in a state that was either prior to the indictment being raised or at the same time as it was raised but that since you had the presumption of innocence at the time, you could use your assets, all of them, as you pleased. So tomorrow I shall report this to my fellow judges to let them know what your position is, and I sincerely hope that with them I'll arrive at a solution so that you can have a lawyer representing you at trial. No need to pass the floor to anybody because you have already expressed your views in writing. Mr. Karnavas, you filed a motion or your answer a very comprehensive one for Mr. Prlic and this will make our work very easy because we can issue an informed decision, because this is very much at the heart of the rights of the Defence. Second item, preparation for trial. As you know, some months ago, I issued an order to the OTP directing within the framework of the -- preparing the pre-trial brief the witness list and the combatant list, directing them to set up a sheet, a table, with various columns. Why? I wanted to have this kind of schedule so that myself and the judges assisting me in this trial have a comprehensive idea, an informed idea, of the charges against the Accused. I want to stress once again that the Accused still benefit from the presumption of innocence. Sometime ago I received the witness list, the exhibit list, and the pre-trial brief from the OTP. I looked into them and I noted that my directions were not quite complied with. More specifically, I am unable to cross-reference the witnesses, the exhibits and the various paragraphs of the indictment, not to speak of the pre-trial brief. As a reminder, in this trial, and this is a mega trial, which is quite unique in the history of this Tribunal. The only large trial there was was the Kupreskic case. There were six of them -- I mean accused -- but this only actually dealt with two facts, allegedly taking place in Ahmici in 1992 and in April 1993. So basically there were two facts. And the Trial Chamber in the Kupreskic case came to a guilty finding on this. So in the Kupreskic case, I do invite everyone present here to read the Kupreskic judgement. You will see that there are very few references to exhibit lists and now, if I remember well, if there were 56 Prosecution witnesses, all of them were heard but they are hardly referred to in the judgement. So the Kupreskic precedent has nothing to do with this instant case. For the time being, we have 10.000 exhibits. There were 9.490 initially and no later than late last week we got some more, some 400 additional documents from the ECMM. So we've reached the 10.000 mark whether it comes to exhibits. Some of them are hundreds of pages long. So we as judges and you as counsel, Defence counsel, you have a mountain of documents facing you. On the other hand -- well, of course, the Defence did put forward their arguments but the Prosecution aiming for 400 witnesses viva voce or under 92 bis. As to those under 92 bis, the Defence have challenged all of them. My Chamber will have to issue a decision on this, and it may be that the 400 witnesses will have to come and testify here. As you know, under the Rules, as a Pre-Trial Judge, I am under the obligation to make sure that this process -- that this trial can be held without delay and to take all necessary steps. But on top of this, and this I failed to see in the filings I received this morning from the Prosecution, under the rules, in Rule 73 bis(C), my Chamber, in the light, so my Chamber will have to decide and determine the number of witnesses the Prosecutor may call, as well as the time available to the Prosecutor for presenting evidence. So how -- how can I determine the number of witnesses and the time available for their testimony if I do not have a clear idea of the relevance of their testimony and of the likely content of that testimony with regard to the indictment as spelled out in the pre-trial brief? I can't just give a free for all or carte blanche to the Prosecutor and say, okay, 400 witnesses, fine. These are your witnesses. I have to check why such witnesses are relevant inasmuch as they relate to the indictment. Let me quote a decision of 21st of January 2003, and I note in this decision, that this related to the Blagojevic case. Mr. Karnavas was the counsel representing Blagojevic so he knows this inside out. And in a nutshell, the Defence, that is Mr. Karnavas, objected to the fact that the Blagojevic Chamber should have Prosecution material. Judge Schomburg was the Presiding Judge. He's now on the Appeals Chamber and Judge Agius, he's now in this Trial Chamber and that Chamber issued a decision. I'm going to quote some whereases which are going to explain to you why I insist on a schedule. So this is what the Trial Chamber then said. "Noting that the Rules do not merely reflect the common law system or the inquisitorial system of the civil law, that this Tribunal does not rely on one system but is a combination of both, with, as a primary objective to ensure a fair and expeditious trial." "So the Rules are there to make it possible to have a fair and expeditious trial, noting that the material requested by the Chamber is necessary for the Chamber to deal more efficiently with the obligation it is under pursuant to the Rules, noting that the requested material by the Chamber will make it possible to have a better trial management, helping the Chamber to issue decisions during the trial, noting that the requested material will not be regarded as evidence by the Trial Chamber, as long as it is not submitted and adduced into evidence at the trial." So I repeat that. "This material will help the Pre-Trial Judge to fulfil its obligation -- his obligations under 55 ter, Rule 55 ter, since the requested material will make it possible for the Chamber to fulfil its obligations under Rule 73 bis, including the obligation of seeing whether you have to shorten the estimated length of the examination-in-chief for some witnesses, to determine the number of witnesses the Prosecutor may call and the time available for the Prosecution for presenting evidence." So this is in a few words what the Chamber said then, its conclusion, and this is what I'm going to do precisely tomorrow. I'm going to ask the Prosecution to provide me with all prior statements and copies of the 10.000 exhibits. I want copies on paper, not on a CD-ROM. Why do I ask that? Because, you know, 10.000 exhibits, 400 witnesses, I have to make a connection between the exhibits and the witnesses. I was curious intellectually to look, to cast a glance at the facts as alleged in the indictment. The factual allegations are to be found again in the pre-trial brief by the Prosecution because in the said brief you have annexed to it, municipality by municipality, you have various annexes, 1, 2, 3, et cetera, that mention a number of facts. The facts are such by way of an example for the Prozor municipality, in the Prosecution document, you have 175 facts. In theory, all of them have to be established by way of an exhibit or by -- through a witness. And I went further than that. I went beyond the pre-trial brief, together with my legal assistants. I searched very thoroughly for mentions in the indictments of certain municipalities. Again, I'll give you an example. The municipality where you have the least facts. That's Gornji Vakuf municipality. So, there, as you know, you have several counts mentioned in the indictment, and as you know, all in all, for the Gornji Vakuf municipality, you have 23 of them, but there is actually in a relevant way, not 23, there is 11 of them, and of the 11 counts, I see that it covers actually more than that municipality. It covers several of them. You've got Hrasnica, Uzricje, sorry for the pronunciation, Zdrimci, Dusa. There is at least four villages involved, and this allegedly took place on the 18th of January 1991. There were attacks, there was looting, burning, a population transfer. All this since it is in the indictment must be proven, at least through witnesses or exhibits. Now, if you have 10.000 exhibits, those you are providing me with, and with these 400 witnesses, how can I know which is the witness, which is the exhibit that deals precisely with Gornji Vakuf? Only you can do this with a schedule. And this is in your interest. In this way, you will know where you're going. It is the interest of the Defence because legally speaking the Defence teams are entitled to know what charges are brought against -- or are going to be dealt with through which witnesses in order to prepare their cross-examination and it will be in the interest of the judges because then they will have a comprehensive idea of what the various pieces contain, the indictment, the pre-trial brief, what they encompass. This morning I received filings from the OTP and you say that you cannot do this job, whilst in my order I had said that you had until the 25th of February. So you've got more than three weeks left to do the job. As long as I do not have this, I cannot have convened the Chamber for it to ascertain the number of witnesses and the length of each testimony. I just wanted to tell you this. I'm now speaking to the Prosecution. To avoid any misunderstanding of the intentions of the Pre-Trial Judge, he has a to prepare a file to be submitted to the Trial Chamber, Trial Chamber II. So the other two fellow judges who are going to be ad litem Judges who are going to be assigned to this case. As long as I don't have this, I am not able to ask my fellow judges to make a decision under Rule 73 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Of course, given this mountain of documents, and the large number of witnesses, the Defence will have to prepare their cross-examination, and if there is -- if it's so opaque, how could they prepare their cross-examinations? Would the Prosecution have anything to say now orally? Because this is a huge problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, first off Your Honour, I think it's important for the Chamber to understand that the Prosecution is fully prepared to go to trial at such time as three things occur. That is, when all the pending motions are resolved, which are a substantial number of pending motions, some of which have been pending since April of 2005, when the full Trial Chamber is in place with the actual judges who can help and assist Your Honour to address these final preparation tasks, and thirdly, when we have a date certain, all of us, including the Defence, a date certain we can work backward from in order to make all the final preparations such as the organisation of witnesses. When and if those three things occur, Your Honour, the Prosecution is fully prepared to go to trial. The filings that we have made last week on the 19th of January in our witness list and our exhibit list fully complied with the Rule requirements and have indeed provided Your Honour and the other judges of this Chamber, Judge Agius and Judge Parker, with detailed information as to the Prosecution case. The Chamber -- or, excuse me, Your Honour has just indicated in the last few minutes the need to connect the witnesses, the approximately 400 witnesses, to the counts and paragraphs of the indictment. What we have filed, what we filed last week, Your Honour, does exactly that. The 65 ter witness list that the Prosecution has filed indicates by the paragraph of the indictment and the count which witnesses go to which count and which paragraph of the indictment. I should also clarify, if the Chamber has not seen this perhaps already, the pre-trial brief is structured in such a way, and intentionally so, so that the paragraphs in the -- the operative paragraphs in the pre-trial brief are exactly the same as the paragraphs in the amended indictment. So that if one refers to the paragraph in the amended indictment it is the same paragraph in the pre-trial brief by number. This provides the Chamber with extensive information as to the witnesses. Also, Your Honour has indicated that time estimates are needed in order for you to better manage the trial. In every instance, as to the witnesses, we have provided the Chamber a time estimate as required by Rule 65 ter(E)(ii). Those are all been provided and the Chamber has that. As to the exhibits, we have proposed in a filing that we made with Your Honour today, with the Chamber today, and not only -- I should say, not only with you, Judge Antonetti, but also for the consideration of Judge Agius, the presiding Judge, and also Judge Parker a proposed alternative chart which would -- by which the Prosecution would list the exhibits or link the exhibits to the counts and paragraphs of the indictment in the same way. That is done with the witnesses. And we provide that chart to you and your staff and indicated in order to do that, by our time estimates, given the -- well, come back to the number of exhibits in a minute but given the voluminous number of exhibits in this case, that we will indeed endeavour to do that, to assist the Chamber, but that it is not possible, it was not possible yesterday, it is not possible today, and it will not be possible tomorrow, to make that filing by the 25th of February and we have given you an indication that we believe, based upon tower assessment and we have looked at this, we worked with this material for a very long time, and that we believe we can hopefully complete that additional alternative chart which is attached to today's filing, we hope we can provide that to you by approximately the 14th of April. And that will be the time required to do it. So we are happy to work with the Chamber, of course, to move this case and make it as efficient as possible but we cannot do the impossible and that is the time that will be required to provide the alternative chart that we have given to Your Honour today. Just to clarify on the exhibit situation, the motion concerning the ECMM documents, those documents were already listed in the -- in our 65 ter witness list, those exhibits are not in addition to, they are already included within the 9.490 documents, so they were not new nor additional exhibits. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling me that your filings have been done today. I haven't received them. As soon as I see them, I'll look into them. And you telling me that you can do the work but according to your estimation, it cannot be done until the 14th of April. I do take note of what you've just said. However, I read your pre-trial brief with great attention and interest, and the way it is structured makes me think that it is based on three factors, three major factors. Factor one, the joint criminal enterprise factor. The joint criminal enterprise, of course, has an objective, and you also need to have the mens rea, the intention of all members of the joint criminal enterprise. This is something that arises from the Tadic case law, and it can be presented in three forms. I suppose therefore that through its witnesses and its documents, the Prosecution is going to try and show that there was a joint criminal enterprise. I can't find any trace of it whatsoever in the witnesses or the exhibits. Second factor in your pre-trial brief, you then analyse individual liability for each of the Accused, who allegedly planned, ordered, perpetrated, et cetera. That, too, normally it has to be proved through documents or witnesses. Third factor. In the pre-trial brief, this is what I would coin murders in various locations, persecution, looting, et cetera, all that has to be proved as well. And there must be a nexus between the criminal enterprise, the Accused, their behaviour, their actions, and the crimes, under 26 counts, and I'm bound to tell you, I have to tell you that reading your pre-trial brief and the documents I've received raised some questions in my mind as to the way we are going to manage this trial. How do you plan the testimony, the appearance of your witnesses? Are you going to have the expert witnesses first in order to set up the political context, the international armed conflict, the parts played by various actors, and then are you going to go municipality by municipality to look into all the underlying crimes? I'd like to see it clearly, and I believe that the Defence also want to have some clarity. And so far I have no indication from you. And if I had a chart like the one I expected, I should receive this information, and I was interested to read that you plan to have various experts, so I suppose that some of them will speak to the political context. Fine. But when are they going to come? Are they going to be in the beginning, towards the middle, or towards the end of the proceedings? I'd like to know that sort of thing. My memory -- I think you have five hours planned for one expert. That's five hours for the Prosecution, of course. The Defence will tell me in a minute how they plan to cross-examine the witness. But all this has to be prepared in advance. We can't start a trial without knowing where we are going. So -- I know that counsel want to take the floor. You'll have the floor in a minute but first, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are very anxious, and happy to have that sort of dialogue with Your Honour and the other members of the Chamber. I apologise for the filing today that obviously I take completely for granted that you've not had a chance to fully digest it and take it on board especially since, obviously, we were not able to translate it into French this morning. But I should say, Your Honour, make it very clear, that we felt driven by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not necessary to have these documents translated. I can read them in English. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We were driven very much by the instruction in your order last week to advise the Chamber, as soon as possible, I think were the literal words, at least in the English translation of Your Honour's order, and felt that we needed to get that before the Chamber even prior to there hearing today so that there would be, indeed, no misunderstanding or confusion on these points. In that filing that we made today, among other things, Your Honour, we proposed in a very broad way, of course, what our presentation of the evidence would look like, and it would, indeed, start with a number of overview witnesses, including some of the experts, not all of them because we think some of the experts would fit better elsewhere in other parts of the case but certainly as to what might be called a political or historical witness and some other witnesses about the structures of the HVO, for example, the Croatian Defence Council, we would, indeed, anticipate calling or plan to call such witnesses early in the trial, along with other witnesses that will talk about the general overview, the joint criminal enterprise, the vision of a greater Croatia as pursued by President Franjo Tudjman and these Accused and others, and put that before the Chamber in an extensive and detailed way. Following that evidence, Your Honour, we would present the remainder of our case, largely - I'm sure not perfectly - but largely in a chronological order by the events in the municipalities. That -- and following against, once again, the structure of the indictment. Prozor would be the first municipality, because of the events that happened there in October of 1992. That would then take us to Gornji Vakuf and the events that happened there in -- and other places for that matter, but particularly in Gornji Vakuf in January and February of 1993. That would then take us to Sovici Doljani and the events in April 1993 and so on. I won't take the Court's time to go through it in every detail. I should perhaps on Gornji Vakuf just to clarify any misunderstanding or confusion that we may have caused to Your Honour, when you refer to several towns and villages in Gornji Vakuf, there, of course, is the municipality or the opstina of Gornji Vakuf and within the municipality there are a number of villages and towns that were involved in those events. So it is not an error in the indictment by any means but a description of both the municipality and towns and villages, of course, that bear a number of different names. Now, there is one major qualification to what I've just said and this again is in our paper that we filed this morning. That is this: As I'm sure Your Honour knows from your own experience, it is usually the case that most witnesses touch upon more than one aspect of the case. And indeed in this case, I can tell you, and in a general way, I'm not going to name witnesses this afternoon, but I can tell you there will be witnesses, for example, who were first arrested in connection with the events in Sovici/Doljani in April of 1993. They were then taken to the Ljubuski prison where they were in the Prosecution's views mistreated and mishandled. They were then transferred to the Heliodrom prison and at either or both of those locations they were taken out to various locations to perform illegal forced labour. And those were four distinct aspects of the Prosecution case. And I'm -- I can only assume, Your Honour, that you -- that the Tribunal would not have me bring back the same witness four times to give only that part of the evidence at any given moment which related to that part of the case where we are. So it's essential and it's necessary, unless we do that, unless we call witnesses separately each time for each part of the case, it's inevitable that when we call our witnesses we will be talking about what happened in Sovici Doljani in April of 1993 and attempting to present our case as logically and chronologically as possible, but immediately you'll have a situation where then you're at Ljubuski, then you're at the Heliodrom, and then you're at forced labour locations. So I have to give you that clarification. But subject to that problem, that inherent difficulty in the evidence, we will present the case to you roughly in the way that I have presented to you this afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm very glad to hear that the document I have not received, that has been filed today, that this document will answer a number of concerns I had. As soon as I get hold of this document, I will read it very carefully in order to be fully reassured. I've spoken a lot. The Prosecution has also talked a lot. But, of course, the Defence will have the floor. We'll start with Mr. Karnavas and then we'll finish with Mr. Praljak. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First I want to salute you for seeing the essence of the -- the complexity of this particular case, the volume of documents, and the challenges that the Defence faces. I dare say the Prosecution's motion that was filed today may not be as helpful as they may have represented. It may be so. I don't know. I'm not so sure. I'm also happy that the -- that I was able to be of some assistance given my position in the Blagojevic case, a position that was contrary to what Judge Schomburg wanted at the time. However, in light of the system that was adopted, certainly wiser heads prevailed and so be it. And I'm glad that the order came -- the decision in that case came the way it did because now at least in this particular case, you have sought fit to request from the Prosecution the necessary documents and the outline of the case that would assist you in preparing for your task, which is to make sure that you narrow the case to the very issues that are at hand and also provide you with the necessary background so you can participate in your right and obligation to question witnesses and examine documents that either side may have failed or for whatever reason chosen not to use, documents or questions that might be of assistance in determining the truth in this case. Having said that, I too am concerned with respect to the Prosecution's time line. We must understand that they've had eight years or more to put this case together. This is the culmination of many, many cases. They chose the time and the place whether they were going to indict. They close how they wished to present their indictment. This case was scheduled and slotted for trial around October last year. Then we were told sometime around November then it became December, then February, now we are looking at March, now they are saying pursuant to an order by the Court, that they, with their legion of Prosecution teams, be it lawyers, be it legal assistants, be it analysts, experts, in-house experts and so on, that they need until April. And, of course, what is being sought by the Trial Chamber would be of great assistance to the Defence as well. Now, the problem is, how can we, then, if the Prosecution needs until April, how can we, the Defence, adequately prepare? Especially if we don't have the sort of precise outline that was requested by you in our last Status Conference as to how the case is going to proceed in somewhat detail. Why? In no given case of it this magnitude can a Defence lawyer prepare for the entire case from start to finish by the beginning of the case. You obviously need to prepare as much as you can, especially for the big picture, and then, as the trial commences usually you would focus most of your attention on the witness list and usually it should be presented as was suggested by the Trial Chamber, in a topical manner so that it makes it easy for everyone. Especially for the Defence who need to prepare for the day-to-day cross-examination of experts. Now, I don't want to take up too much of your time Your Honour because I wholeheartedly agree with your order and at least in my jurisdictions, the Prosecution would -- might be facing somewhat of a sanction if they didn't comply with an order. We've heard their response. I'm satisfied that they are trying to do everything they possibly can to comply with the judges -- with your order. But if they are having -- if they see it as a Herculean task, think of what it's like to us. Now, last week we did receive their 242-page trial brief. And we got a list of witnesses, and I must tell you I'm a little concerned. Because there are several experts, I'm not going to name names but I'm just going to name what their supposed to testify to. There is an artillery expert, a financial investigator, a historical expert, a handwriting expert, military expert, expert on presidential transcripts, demography, and so on. Reports of which we don't even have. Now, imagine being in a case eight years preparing it and now they are saying they are going to bring in a financial expert in the middle of the trial. How am I supposed to prepare for the cross-examination of an expert of that nature while I'm preparing for everything else? Now, and I've said this in many cases and I'll say it again and I'll keep saying it until the case is over. There is no such thing as equality of arms in this Tribunal. They do the best they can, I understand, but the Defence has limited resources, and for us to be able to at least prepare for the case, even at the very beginning, we need to have these expert reports. We need to have them now. In fact we should have had them yesterday. This was one of the reasons why I was a little, as you may recall, I said I was somewhat disappointed last time in that we didn't hold the Prosecution's feet to the fire and demand that the pre-trial brief be submitted by December. They got an extra month, but now we are facing this particular challenge, and I am concerned. And I know that Your Honour would like to have these reports as well because you need to read them, digest them, so you can be able to participate as well in the process. But there are other statement that we don't have. We know for a fact that they have been interviewing and they continue to interview even probably as we are speaking today they are interviewing vital witnesses. Those statements of which we don't have. When will we be getting these witness statements? Because we will need to do our own investigation. That is a concern as well. And, of course, their documents in the thousands of pages that need to be translate, just for the sake of Mr. Praljak but for the sake of everyone, including yourself, Your Honour. So based on that I just want to raise my concerns. I don't know how we can start the trial as we thought we would, probably at the -- sometime in March or April. I certainly would like to begin as quickly as possible but at the same time I don't want to disadvantage anyone. Certainly not Mr. Praljak. Though I concur with all of your remarks regarding the fact that he does need to have lawyers who are probably going to need some extra time. On the other hand, I don't want to be asked -- standing here asking for a lengthy continuance because I don't know when I'll be getting there material, how much time I will need, because I don't want to make a frivolous request for the sake of making a frivolous request. I've been working diligently full time on this case since the moment I got into it. So that's another consideration. These are the sort of things that at some point we need to iron out. I agree with Mr. Scott that it would be helpful for us to have a date certain but I think to choose a date certain at this point in time, without having all of this information doesn't really -- isn't that very helpful. I think what might be necessary is for the Court to impose a date certain by which the Prosecution will turn over all of the evidence that they intend to use at trial. All of it. Unfortunately we don't have the French system where you have a dossier, we know this is the universe of all the documents. So the investigation continues. Fine. But at least to the extent that they list witnesses that they expect to testify, particularly as expert witnesses, some of whom work for the Prosecution, they are employees of the UN. I hesitate to call them experts. They are analysts, they are OTP employees but they are going to come in here testifying as quote unquote experts. But nonetheless, where are their reports? Some of them have been around for many, many years and I don't want to be engaged in a trial where my client is going to be disadvantaged and I'm being put in a position where I have to effectively provide ineffective assistance of counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm being asked to do a disservice to my client because I'm being put in a position of having to rush through and not being -- be thoroughly prepared. I believe that the Prosecution, with respect to my client and other clients are going to be asking at the conclusion of the case a sentence that would literally cause them to die in prison. That's a serious matter. And given that, given the importance of what we have, and this case covers a long period, there is historical, there is political, there is economic, there is financial, you name it, there are all sorts of different issues and I know that they have been working very, very hard and I'm not trying to say that they are doing anything that is not proper. But I think that perhaps they need to be directed to provide all of this information, perhaps we need to have a joint meeting with the Chambers, like a 65 ter meeting where we might be able to hash some of these things out. But I can tell you, Your Honour, I intend to challenge a lot of this stuff that they want to come in, you know, all these documents without any proof, it's UN so therefore it's -- we should take judicial notice of them, or the European monitors therefore let's just bring it all in by the truckload without witnesses. I mean, I intend to challenge all of that because I want to make sure that my client as well as every other client in this case gets a fair trial and I think that's exactly what you intend to do in this case. So with those remarks, Your Honour, I want to thank you again for seeing the difficulties that the Defence has in this particular case. They are monumental. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Second lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that I echo a lot of the comments that Mr. Karnavas made, all of them actually. What I find particularly difficult with respect to the submission that the OTP made is that the Court ordered the OTP to make it in a certain way. And specifically with reference to documents with 9700 some documents I'd like to know that I don't have to read every one of those 9700 documents if 5.000 of those documents aren't connected to my client and my client's portion of the case. I don't know that. I have to look at all the documents. If the submission had been made the way the Court had ordered it by linking the documents to the witnesses to the events, then it would save -- would have saved us a lot of work. I mean, if you just think you just preliminarily looking at one documents for 60 seconds, there is 9700 documents, I mean, that's just immense, not to mention some of those documents which my client can't read because they are in English, or in another language that he doesn't understand. So I think -- I'm sure that the Prosecution -- I mean obviously we've heard from them today, are doing their best to try to get whatever they think is appropriate to the parties but the Court ordered it one way and we didn't get it in that way. And I'm a little disappointed in that from my perspective. It just makes a lot of work. We already have a lot of work but it makes a lot of work for us. The other issue that Mr. Karnavas touched upon was the issue of trial, and we did see somewhat of a suggested date by the OTP in their latest filing which you'll see Your Honour, I just had a chance to skim it just now. But I think it would be beneficial notwithstanding the difficulties that are going to be encountered by the OTP in getting these documents in the form that the Court requested to all parties, and notwithstanding the issue of Mr. Praljak, to set a date certain, and I don't know if the Court can even do that now under the circumstances, as the Court has explained to us. But having a date certain and working back from that I think puts a little bit more pressure on people to get things done but, you know, in my view, looking at this case the Court had initially there was some suggestions that the case could be tried in March and I just don't see that happening in all honesty. We need to have some fixed date that we can work back from and I don't know if Your Honour is interested in doing that and we've haven't really discussed that generally among counsel but I think that would help in some instances, sort of put a little bit of pressure on everyone to have a date certain. The other thing that the Court had requested that we do and I don't think Mr. Scott mentioned it was that we sit and discuss some of these issues before land which we did before today's status conference. We did sit and talk about the methodology of questioning and time limits and things like that. And we have an understanding, we haven't come into any sort of agreement but we've come to understanding of, okay there is a good starting point, let's work on further trying to refine it so we can present it to Your Honour and to the Chamber. So in light of those things, Your Honour, I guess that's all I have to say. I don't want to repeat what Mr. Karnavas said but I think you understand our concerns. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, third lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to join in the positions of my colleagues and I will be very brief. I have only four points to present in relation to this subject. First of all, I think it is very important that the OTP act in accordance with instructions issued by the Court and indeed to make a survey of this voluminous material so that we could find our way through this abundance of material, both we the Defence and the Court. Secondly, as for the 92 bis witnesses, their statements have not been submitted. In relation to witnesses, I also wish to say that there are some witnesses who are supposed to testify viva voce but we still don't have their statements. We will try to deal with this directly in contacts with the OTP. However, my fourth point which causes particular concern is suspect statements that are provided as reliable information. So when a certain person is to be heard as a witness, we are actually admitting a statement that the said person gave as a suspect. And on the basis of that suspect interview, we draw certain conclusions related to the indictment itself, various counts, et cetera. I think that this is impermissible practice and I would like to draw the attention of the Court to it, and also to the impermissibility of providing one type of statement, that is to say suspect interviews, to be admitted as relevant trial material pertaining to a particular witness. Thirdly, if the Prosecution is allowed more time for preparing the necessary motions, I suggest that the Defence's time be extended as well. Also, we fully subscribe to what our colleagues said, that once we receive all this material from the Prosecution, the Defence be given sufficient time to prepare this very complex case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Valentin Coric fully supports what our colleagues say, that is to say Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Kuzmanovic, and Ms. Alaburic. I would just like to state that we think that the Trial Chamber should insist on the documents of the 30th of November 2005. May I remind you that Appeals Chamber in the Kupreskic case that you referred to yourself pointed out that the role of the pre-trial brief is not to provide a digested version of the indictment but that on the contrary it is a very important trial document whose primary task is to help the Trial Chamber and the Defence to prepare for the case and trial properly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Pusic fully subscribes to the views presented by our other colleagues. I just wish to say that the list that you ordered the Prosecution to produce is very important for yet another reason as well, and that is time. Time is an important factor in this trial. We have six Accused persons and then there is the Prosecution and everybody is going to require time. If we work out this table or this list properly, then we will deal with this as efficiently as possible and we will resolve matters properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Praljak, before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm in a good position here, I think, to say something. Regardless of what the Prosecution thinks, I emerged from the war convinced, with the wisdom I have, that I did what I did with a maximum of high moral standards. Perhaps I'm wrong. But for ten years now, we have been living under pressure and for another ten years perhaps we will live under this pressure that perhaps we are war criminals. Believe me, I'd like to find that out. Relatively soon at that, and in a just manner. So that my family, my friends, my grandchildren, would not live that way for 20 years, and that's as long as it's going to take. Namely, that it is possible that we are the most serious of war criminals. The way the Prosecutor presented list case now is that now, on your part, after eight years of investigation, what is the result? Je m'en fous. Secondly you say in the indictment that all members of the HDZ, all members of the HVO, the entire nation at that, is waiting to find out whether, with their representatives, they are all part of a criminal enterprise. Nothing but a criminal enterprise. Taking advantage of such a situation, indicting 99 per cent of the members of that nation, you go down there, you take statements from people for that indictment, that kind of indictment. That is true. You told everyone that they were suspects, that they were possible indictees, and oh, then they are really going to testify freely and fairly. Oh, yes! Your Honours, there are three more remaining matters. I did not give a single euro for the house on (redacted).I returned that apartment to my wife. And I did not have any share in any enterprises during the indictment and after the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before we have a break, because for technical reasons, as we know, we have to have a break, as short as possible. I think that a quarter of an hour will be more than enough. I note at this stage that all counsel have the same position. So there is a united front among the counsel. Mr. Praljak, of course, joins them, with the underlying thought that everybody wants to know when the trial is going to start. We have a few more seconds before the break. I informed the president of the Tribunal and my two colleagues of Trial Chamber II that I thought it was very unlikely that we could start early March because of there counsel issue. This issue has to be settled as quickly as possible. Once it is settled, we will have made a major step forward. However, we'll have to meet again in February for further hearings, for technical hearings, forensic hearings. I was told that Courtroom I, II, or III would not be available, which means that we could convene in Room 398 or 396, where you can have interpretation into the three languages, but if Mr. Praljak still hasn't got a lawyer by then, for him not to have to come here we could have a video conference from Zagreb. But then the Registry would have to help me out and give me further explanations. Anyway, this would take place in February, and I think we have to meet at least twice in February, for several hours at a time. It's now quarter to four. We are going to have a break for a quarter of an hour. We shall resume at 1600 hours sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing resumed, and I'm now going to deal with pending requests, pending motions. Before moving on to that particular issue let me just point out a specific point related to translation. As you know, when you speak in English here what you say is translated into French and B/C/S. When I speak in French what I stay is translated into B/C/S directly or into English and then B/C/S. But what matters, if there is any problem at all is to refer to the audio recording of the proceedings. Otherwise there might still be an uncertainties remaining. Let me give you an example. Before the last Status Conference, before the end of the last Status Conference I said the following: "We've dealt with all points on the agenda, the hearing stands adjourned," and when I read the transcript in French, I saw the following: "Meaning because I'm exhausted, I have to adjourn the meeting." So what we should refer to is the audio recording, what is authoritative is the audio recording. If we ever need to go back to the original material we should go back to the audio recording of the proceedings. Now, let me move on to the list of pending motions. The Accused Praljak has made a number of filings, filed a number of motions related to the translation of the pre-trial brief and of exhibits. Mr. Praljak is representing himself so he should receive all documents in his own language. Therefore, the time limit he gets to answer, to respond, is set at the 15th of March. He has until the 15th of March to give his response to the pre-trial brief. That's his particular deadline. As for the motion by Mr. Praljak from the 5th of January 2006, I've dealt with it already so I'm not going to deal with it again. We also have a motion by the Prosecution related to judicial notice in relation to rules 89(C) and others. This is dated 27th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Accused Stojic has answered late to this motion because he received the motion at his office but he was not at his office. In any case, the Prosecution according to the Prosecution, Mr. Stojic has filed beyond the time limits that had been set. But let me remind you that according to Rule 126 bis, the time of 14 days starts running from the day the motion has been filed with the Registry. So once a motion has been filed with the Registrar, you have 14 days to respond, and if a reply is to be requested, then you should ask for authorisation to do so and then you will be granted seven days to reply. So please remember that the time for answering or responding to a motion is 14 days and seven days for a reply. With relation to this motion filed under 94(A) and 89(C), I was waiting for the pre-trial brief with a list of exhibits and the list of witnesses. I was waiting to receive that before submitting the matter to my fellow judges and before submitting a draft decision to them. So now this will happen very quickly. Since the 4th of April 2005, we have a pending motion for judicial notice related to other cases under Rule 94(B). All the parties have responded to the motion. Additional responses have also been filed -- well the conclusion of all this is that there is absolutely no agreement between the parties as relates to 94(B), Rule 93(B). The Trial Chamber will very soon make a decision with regard to that issue. On the 27th of December the Prosecution filed a motion asking the Defence to notify under 67(A) any Defence of alibi or any special defence. A number of Accused have responded to that motion. As you know, the Defence is under no obligation to respond or to invoke a defence of alibi before the trial, at any time. The Defence can use that type of defence evening during the presentation of the Defence case. So there is no urgency there. Let me remind you that we have two parts in Rule 67, the defence of alibi and if I sum up, it's the case of an Accused who produces an alibi saying, "I am -- it's alleged that I was at such and such a place but I was not there, I was somewhere else." That's the defence of alibi. The special item in this Rule is special defence including a number of situations but that's the case where an Accused was under a -- an attenuation of his mental responsibility at the time the facts were committed, and he produces certificates to ascertain this. So that's for Rule 67 and the Chamber will also issue a decision with relation to this motion. We also have three confidential motions. I can deal with them because I'm not going to name any names of witnesses. This is related to 92 bis for A, B, C and D. I'm not going to go into detail about this, but we've received a number of responses and a decision will be taken. But I note that the Defence unanimously has refused, rejected, these testimonies and has demanded that the witnesses come and testify live. All the Defence has submitted that these testimonies relate to the facts and behaviour of the Accused and not -- do not fall under the purview of 92 bis. I'm considering all of this at the moment. I'm also going to submit a draft decision to my fellow judges very soon. We also have a motion, a confidential motion, by the Prosecution related to ECMM documents. I received this motion this morning only, and naturally the Defence will have to respond and has 14 days to respond to that motion. Let me also mention the confidential motion related to the removal of a statement by an Accused. We will also deal with that motion and rule on that motion. We also have a confidential motion related to the production of documents addressed to Croatia. Croatia has given a response. We've had a response by the ambassador of Croatia to Trial Chamber I, but apparently the document got lost, although I've found it again, so we have all the necessary documents. There is also another motion but I can't mention it in open session. I'll come back to that later. We also have a motion from January 24th requesting from the Chamber that it should deal with the matter of the translation of documents falling under Rules 66 and 68. Now, about this specific matter, which is a very common issue raised here at the Tribunal, my personal position, which I also have in the Seselj case, is the following: When you have an Accused who is representing himself, he should have in his own language all documents pertaining to Rules 66 and 68, documents that will be used by the Prosecution when examining their witnesses. It would not be understandable for a Accused who is representing himself not to have in advance all the exhibits that will be submitted to Prosecution witnesses. It's unthinkable. So that's my personal position. It's very clear. And nothing will make me change my mind on that issue. When you have an Accused who is representing himself, that Accused should have at his disposal all the documents that will be submitted to the witness when the witness comes to testify. Trial Chamber II will very soon render a decision pertaining to a motion in Seselj, in the Seselj case, but as for the pending motion filed by the Prosecution, this is my position, my personal position. If my colleagues share my view, then there will be no problem. If my colleagues do not share my view, then I will write a dissenting opinion in the direction that I've just outlined for you. I should also mention, we only have 45 minutes left, but let me ask the Registrar to move into private session very quickly, or very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line with what I've just said, in November, I referred to my colleagues a request for the delegation of powers of the Chamber under Rule 73. Why? Because I believe that the preparation and the management of a megatrial should mean that the Pre-Trial Judge is personally involved in the case and that's what I've been doing on a daily basis over the past three months, and the Pre-Trial Judge should also have a certain room for manoeuvre, allowing him -- under the control of the Trial Chamber, allowing him to make decisions that do not involve any academic questions and that is, for example, the case of the amendments of the conditions of pre-trial detention or pre-trial release. There is no need to refer the matter to all the three judges, according to me. I'll deal with that with my colleagues tomorrow. I know that they have a very busy schedule themselves because of other cases but the management of a -- megatrials has been dealt with in Canada by a special commission and the question asked was how to manage a megatrial? The conclusion reached by this commission that existed in 2003 and 2004, was that when you have a megatrial, you should adapt some of the provisions of the rules and various codes to these mega trials. You should move slightly away from the habitual rules, and the commission submitted a number of recommendations, among them the assignment of a judge in charge of the management of the trial. In our Rules, we have a Pre-Trial Judge. So he prepares the trial. And in Canada, they dealt with that issue also. But as for -- up until now, here at the Tribunal, we -- no one had thought about that particular issue, but since the work conducted by the commission headed by Judge Bonomy, we have come to realise that it is absolutely essential for a Pre-Trial Judge to become very involved in the pre-trial stage. I've listened very carefully to what the Prosecution had to say when they reminded us that the Chamber is made up of three judges. Yes, I'm very well aware that a claim is made up of three judges but you should also not forget that the Trial Chamber judging the case will not be made up of these three judges. There will be me as the Presiding Judge and two or three ad litem Judges. So you have to understand that Judge Parker or Judge Agius will not be sitting on this trial at the trial stage. You'll be dealing with three new judges. Furthermore, as for the beginning of a trial, opening date of a trial, I want to be very open towards all parties in this case. Ad litem judges an appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations two weeks only before the beginning of the trial. In other words, the ad litem judges who will come here will have two weeks, 15 days, to read 10.000 exhibits, thousands of pages, 400 witnesses, et cetera. So you have to be aware of that. In any case, if the trial begins on the 1st of March, they will be appointed on the 15th of February if the trial starts on the 1st of April they will be appointed on the 15th of March, and if the trial starts on the 1st of May they will be appointed on the 15th of April. That's the information I can give you about the dates, and as I said earlier on, things will become much clearer once the issue of the counsel has been solved. Let me now move to the issues on the agenda of our meeting. Now for the disclosure of exhibits related to Rules 66 and 68, it seemed to me that listening to the Defence, it seemed to me that what they were saying, the tone of what they were saying, was that they did not have the witness statements. So it seems to me that there are still a few problems when it comes to the production or disclosure of evidence. So I'll turn first to the Prosecution to see where we stand on that point and then I'll give the floor to the Defence. Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We did deal with this issue when we met with the Defence shortly before this Status Conference. Due to the fact that the Prosecution only finalised and completed its witness list shortly before the 19th of January when we filed that list, there are a few outstanding witness statements that -- and related material relating to those witnesses that has yet to be disclosed. We are currently in the process of compiling that material and will be in a position, we believe, to make that final Rule 66 disclosure very shortly. Again, we are aware of a number of statements that have yet to be disclosed, at least one of my colleagues from the Defence have identified some other statement that we believe have been disclosed but which they have been unable to locate among the material that has been disclosed so we are undertaking a further review to determine precisely what material needs to be disclosed pursuant to Rule 66 and, as I indicated, are in the process of making sure that that disclosure occurs as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me now listen to the Defence. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very briefly. First I want to compliment Mr. Mundis for that clear answer. Yes they have provided us to the best that they can. However, there are two points that I want to make. First there is the list on their Pre-Trial brief. Of course, we want to make sure that we have all those statements. But I want to have every single statement that they've taken of any witness or suspect that they have and I know for a fact that some gave statements, well, months and months and months ago. So I ask myself, Why am I not getting it? What's the problem? Why can't I have it earlier? There might be something in it that might be helpful for me, I don't know. I'm sure if it was very hurtful I might have it. Maybe it's being held back. I don't want to read into what's going on but I want to make sure I have everything that they have as part of their investigation. What the Court is going to get from what I understand from the Blagojevic decision is what the Prosecution intends to use at trial. That was one of the key issues that I had with Judge Schomburg, that they shouldn't get their entire -- but I think that any statement they have taken relevant to there case, whether they intend to use it at trial or not we are entitled to that. To the extent they can look I would most appreciate it. I want to again stress the fact the Prosecution, in particular Mr. Mundis has been very forthcoming in every request we've made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I know that Mr. Mundis is always very forthcoming so I'm reassured now to hear that. Second lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have made a request from counsel for the Prosecution for the things that we thought we had missing, so hopefully we will be able to work things out in addition to what Mr. Karnavas said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I've already said that we accept -- expect to have direct communication with the OTP and solve our outstanding issues that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Valentin Coric agrees with what Mr. Karnavas has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My experience tells me that Mr. Scott and the other Defence counsel will very speedily fulfill what they have promised to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Accused I agree with what Mr. Karnavas said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now move to an issue that has been of great concern to me. For the past three months, it's the matter of the length of the cross-examination that will be conducted by Defence counsel and possibly by Mr. Praljak if he doesn't have counsel. Cross-examination following the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, I invited the Prosecution and the Defence to meet after the last status conference. I understand that you've met and it seemed to me that from what I've heard, you have been able to reach an agreement. You might be able to confirm that fact to me or not, but in any case, the issue at stake here is as follows: In its pleadings, in its written filings, the Prosecution has told us for witness X we'll need four hours. Four hours, that's one day of hearing almost. What bothers me when we think that this trial should be fair is to know how the six Defence counsel or the five Defence counsel and the Accused will cross-examine the witness. Will they each demand four hours so that would lead to us a total of 24 hours or will they come to agreement, these Defence counsel, to have leading counsel, so to speak, who will lead the cross-examination on their behalf but then another of problems are raised by that option and, of course, the other lawyers would have the opportunity to intervene and ask questions if that was needed. In a civil law system the president -- presiding Judge leads the proceedings so -- and I believe that's the best system. Then that sort of problem does not arise but that's not the system we are working under. And since we have to follow the Rules, and not the system I would prefer, I have to comply with the Rules. Therefore, I would like to know at what stage your discussions have led you. That's why in the next few weeks, I was expecting to meet up with you again in order for us to solve that issue because I believe it's a very, very important issue in a mega trial so let me turn to the specialist, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, as you can imagine and appreciate, I think, we had after the last Status Conference when you suggested that we get together to discuss this topic, one of the immediate problems, of course, was the availability of Mr. Praljak, who upon being informed that we wanted to have these meetings, wrote back to us and said that he very much would like to participate. Given the current state of affairs, we then determined that the best course of action was simply to wait until immediately prior to today's Status Conference so that Mr. Praljak could attend and represent himself at those discussions. I think it's fair to say, and I believe my colleagues across the courtroom will agree with me that our initial meeting on this subject today was very productive. We didn't reach any conclusions nor have we come to any point in these discussions where we can inform Your Honour that we've come to an agreement or a proposal that we could put before you, that there is a -- that there is in effect an agreement between the parties. We are certainly not at that stage, having just had initial discussions, but I do believe, Your Honour, that the meeting was a productive and an open one. I believe it was a very transparent meeting.
