I believe that all of the various parties, all of the Defence teams, were able to put forward their initial views on this issue and I think the next step would be for the Defence teams to discuss a little bit further amongst themselves, perhaps for the Prosecution team to discuss a little bit more within -- on our side, how to go forward, and we do expect within the next couple of weeks, perhaps some further exchanges written correspondence, solidifying the various positions and perhaps from there maybe being able to take it a little bit further in terms of putting before Your Honour a little -- something that's a little bit more concrete in terms of where we stand and at that point it might very well be productive for Your Honour to come in and take perhaps a little bit more an active role in the process. But again we've only had this initial discussion. I believe everyone would agree it was very productive but we don't certainly after one meeting on this subject we don't have a high degree of overlap in terms of interests or a high degree of agreement. But I believe that we'll continue to work in good faith and be able to perhaps hopefully narrow some of the issues so that Your Honour can then play a little bit more of an active role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, if you would like me to play a more active role, of course, I'm quite prepared. I would even say that I would rush into the job. But still, you have to give me the green light to do so because first of all, you need to have an agreement between the parties as to this procedure. As far as I can see, if you don't reach an agreement between the parties, that's one possibility that must be taken into account. Then mathematically, the solution would be a solution maintaining the rights of the defence. Would you have four hours and each of the Defence counsel may request four hours. Because here, this is not a collective liability. We are talking about individual liability, and strategies may be diverse. Issues may be diverse too, their implications as well. It will depend on the one or the other. Therefore, that's what -- where the problem lies. And I believe that everybody can understand this. So ideally speaking, as far as I can see, if you have five or six lawyers, they should agree and that would be perfect. If they don't, then the Trial Chamber, together with my two or three ad litem judges, will have to discuss the issue as quickly as possible. But then we have to look at mathematical solution. Four hours for the Prosecution, then four hours for each of the Accused, of course, there will be repetitions. So maybe the first one will take four hours, less for the others, but that would be the mathematical solution. But the best solution would be agreement among yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, and I think that was the spirit in which these discussion that is we had earlier this afternoon were undertaken. I believe all of the parties put forward their best faith efforts and again it was only an initial meeting and the discussion ranged from whether it should be a time-for-time, Prosecution takes four hours, all of the Defence teams get four hours to split or each of the individual Defence teams gets four hours or some middle ground, if you're working in terms of a mathematical formula or perhaps the other approach would be less focussed on mathematics and more of a focus on efficiency and whether the questions were redundant or repetitive at which point in time the cross-examination might need to come to an end. There are a variety of different ways of looking at the problem and we again have taken that first step to try to explore it amongst ourselves. Partially because it's -- it can be a rather time consuming process and at some point once we've more solid identified our various positions and come to some internal understandings between the Defence teams and again from the Prosecution side, we might be in a much better position to actively seek Your Honour's more active involvement in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I think that the experience gained by Mr. Karnavas in the Blagojevic case might be useful. You have the floor, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First I must say I'm heartened by what I hear and your precision in which you recognise the difficulty we have in that this is not a collective liability instance but everybody has to defend their own client. While I would agree with you that perhaps having the judge ask all the questions might be the best approach I would also argue for an investigative judge in the middle but we don't have that. Be that as it may, I think Mr. Mundis was quite accurate in saying that the meeting was held and everyone put forward their position in good spirit. Obviously there is no mathematical approach that we can take even the one I believe that Your Honour suggested, which might be -- seem fair, I think under the realistic circumstances, some witnesses you need more time, other witnesses you need less. One Accused may need to cross-examine, the other don't. I can assure His Honour that you need not be concerned with respect to this particular Defence or even my colleagues, in that we don't intend to take up time for the sake of taking up time. I think the questions have to be relevant. If the Prosecution chooses not to go into an area because they've chosen for instance to limit their direct examination, that should not prevent me from going into an area, assuming that area is relevant to my defence. That's why the mathematics don't work. There will be instances where the best cross may be no cross-examination because maybe the witness hasn't provided anything. I think we all recognise from the Defence standpoint that it is to our best interest to assist the Tribunal in asking questions and taking up time only when it realistically helps our case. So no questions should be posed if it does not advance the theory of a Defence case. But I agree with His Honour that we have to look at the Defence counsel individually. We are going to meet -- the Defence will meet. We will meet with the Prosecution. I have proposed and I will propose again to my colleagues that it's to our best interests, the Defence, to meet prior to the examination of a particular witness so we can figure out among ourselves what areas any particular individual would need to ask. That way, if one covers the majority of it, they may not wish to go into other areas. It also helps because the last thing we want to do is make the Prosecution's job much easier by hurting each other which is one of the tactics which is used by the Prosecution in joining all these cases hoping that we will be firing our shots at each other, making their job easier, to meet their burden. Hopefully that won't happen. So I can assure His Honour that at least we will -- among ourselves, organise ourselves, so that before every witness we know what we need to cross-examine. We will hopefully have some sort of a game plan and I can assure you, at least from my part, I do not intend to take up any more time. However, what I do believe? That I need extra time. I will be heard because I believe that there are some issues that we need to cover in great detail. So I hope I've answered some of your concerns, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before I give the floor to the other Defence counsel, let me say something between brackets, as it were. I think it is very important, and I do as you all to listen attentively. As I told you earlier on, for the time being, the Prosecution planning to seek to adduce some 10.000 documents that might be tantamount to 100.000 or 200.000 pages, I don't know. Whatever it may be, when a document is admitted as evidence, that document may be 20 pages long. The Prosecution are going to put questions regarding the document to the witness. The Defence will cross-examine the witness on the document in question. And that will be true when we have Defence witnesses. But no, please remember one thing: A document that is admitted as evidence will be looked at, be scrutinised by each and every Judge, and when we issue a judgement, which will be a reasoned judgement, we will rely on certain paragraphs of that one document that may not have been looked into through questions by the Prosecution or by the Defence during cross-examination. In other words, if a document is admitted as evidence in this case, it will be taken into account by the Judges from A to Z. In other words, if you are the cross-examiner, you are supposed to know all of the document. You're supposed to put questions to the witness on the basis of the document. So, please, remember this and keep it in mind: A document, and you know that as well as I do, when there is a witness, things go very fast, very fast indeed, because time goes by, there are a lot of questions, and then there are hundreds of documents, especially so when you have an expert to deal with. So you can imagine the mass of work it represents. You have to know the document. So do not be surprised if, in the judgement, a document is mentioned whilst no question was put to the witness who introduced it on this or that paragraph, because that document is part of the file, just as much as the testimony is. So I just wanted to point this out to you because it is very, very relevant indeed. You have to keep this in mind. Remember how relevant the documents are. So, Mr. Karnavas do you want to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one point, Your Honour, because I must say that I'm really, really glad that you brought this point up. I cannot begin to express my gratitude because this is the exact argument that I make when they want to introduce a document or a statement from a previous case. You'll see sometimes a document will refer to other documents and so you have to look at the footnote and then all of a sudden, when I read the final judgement, I'm going to see something that I might have admitted to that was, you know, it's couched in there. And that's the monumental difficulty that the Defence has, and so I'm glad that you bring this up. That's why I really do not appreciate having thought -- having documents brought in or witness statements brought in because a witness statement looks innocuous maybe but they might have referred to an exhibit and then when you look at that exhibit, it refers to another exhibit. There may be something in there that might come directly back to my client, and therefore what I have done I have agreed to accept, and in essence I've nailed -- put one more nail into my client's coffin that says guilty. I don't want that to happen and I'm glad, Your Honour, that you see the difficulties that we face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I venture to make this observation because as a judge, I had the privilege of also being either a Prosecutor or a Defence counsel before I became a judge. But it means that I have an overall view of the issue. So I call your attention on this issue, and what you've just said is absolutely right. You may cross-examine a witness on a given paragraph but when the Judges assess the probative value of a document, they take it all in. So that, the Defence counsel, is supposed to know the entire document. The second lawyer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Without wasting the Court's time, we have talked I think a loot of the issues that we've already discussed are very important. I would echo the comment of the previous counsel, Mr. Karnavas, and we'll say that we will tried in our first session that lasted probably 45 minutes to work through these issues for the first time. It was productive and I think we are glad and I'm very happy that the Court has seen that if for whatever reason there can't be an agreement, that the Court is willing to allow each individual defendant a certain allotment of time that the Prosecution gets because I think that's very important. I don't think it will come to that under the circumstances but it's nice to know that we have that as a basis to start. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Third lawyer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Along with what my colleagues have already said and which I fully endorse, just one more sentence. I believe that the Defence will come by a joint proposal and we hope that that proposal will be dovetailed with the OTP and the Prosecution and this Court won't have to make a ruling on that question like that but that they will find our joint proposal acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleagues have said exactly what the Defence of Valentin Coric wanted to say so I'll say no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further comments to make. I mentioned a moment ago that time is of the essence in this trial and that is why I underlined the fact that the list to be drawn up by the Prosecution pursuant to your request and guidelines should -- could settle this issue too with respect to cross-examination. It can use it rationally, saving the Court time and all of us others time as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took part in it, yes. What might happen is this: That I am not assigned counsel, which would go against my own wish, of course, because we do believe when they say we believe that I did something and so on but I do hope that I will receive Mr. Kovacic and if so, I will be in detention. This is to be a special situation and, of course, co-counsel Pinter and the Defence will be in good hotels sitting in comfortable armchairs with a glass of wine, I will come from Savica [phoen], and I won't know what they have been discussing and what they decided. So I will examine for my part, as much as I consider necessary, in order to overturn the thesis of the Prosecution. Of course, we must give thought to that, to the fact that that is my proposal, if I'm not given my Defence counsel back, if they are not returned to me. Then my situation and case will be set apart, set aside, and through my lack of legal knowledge -- so that through my lack of legal knowledge I wouldn't do any harm to the Defence cases of the other five Accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think this is all very useful information and this might prompt my fellow judges to make a decision as to the assignment of a counsel for you. Only one quarter of an hour left so we are going to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admissibility of evidence in a previous order as you will realise I took great care to make a distinction between the admissibility and the probative value of evidence. The fact that a document is admitted as evidence does not give it automatically probative value which is determined by Judges after examination-in-chief and cross-examination. And within the framework of the cross-examination, the Defence can very easily argue that the document has no probative value and would seek to reject the document as evidence. When you deal with only 100 or 200 documents, this issue can be settled during trial. But here, we have close to 10.000 documents, in spite of the fact that the Prosecution did not meet all my requests, they made sure to number documents from 1 to 9.400, indicating which of the documents or starting from the oldest in time to the most recent and this time division gives some clarity in and of itself. In the next few days or -- not months, but weeks to come, now we are not talking about months anymore, in the weeks to come, both parties will have to look into this issue. I personally -- I would be in favour of admitting documents from 1 to 9.500 with an exhibit number, P1, 2, and 3, and so on, and when we have the Defence case, with all their documents, there may be 30.000 of them. I don't know, but experience tells me that generally the Defence have more documents than the Prosecution, so if you have 30.000 documents, again, you'll have exhibit numbers. But the fact that a document has a number does not give it sort of top value, probative value, that is. So all this is to avoid discussions when a witness comes to testify, where you would have six Defence lawyers rushing to their feet to say that the document is not relevant. It may not be a relevant document when the Defence says so but that document may be relevant later on, even for the Defence, in a favourable light for the Defence. The fact that you say during trial that is document is not relevant is not useful because you realise how or whether a document has probative value only at the end of the trial. So think it over, because it is absolutely a very essential problem. But this goes back to what I said earlier on. When you have given an exhibit number to a document, that means that the Defence is aware of the entirety of the document and it is up to the Defence to destroy the document by cross-examining on it. And the other way around. When we come to the Defence case, the Prosecution will -- should make sure they study each and every Defence document. So I'm not making a decision now, of course, but think it over. There were other items on the agenda. However, unfortunately, I have no time to deal with them. I wanted to talk about the way documents are submitted to a witness in the courtroom. As you know we've got the e-court system, but as far as I'm concerned, there is only one system I know. It's this: The folder, the binder system. I'm showing it to you. So both parties, faced with a witness, say, "Look, these are the documents, I'm going to submit them to the witness." So here again, think it over. The e-court system is some technological progress. Nevertheless you must be able to feel, taste a document. You must be able to compare it with other documents, and whilst I'm presiding over proceedings, I basically am sitting in a 747 Boeing, you know? I can't sort of press all buttons, you know, to compare documents. I can't do that. However, whilst looking at the screen, while listening to you carefully, I can sort of leaf through a binder. I believe that what I say for myself will apply to my future colleagues on the Bench. So here again you have to think about it. The e-court system was very expensive. It can be useful. But when it comes to documents you must be able to take them in your hands. You have to look at the stamp, the signature. Sometimes you even need to see the original. If, of course, provided the Prosecution or the Defence have the documents. So this was just to outline a few issues, as food for thought for the next few weeks. We are going to move back into private session.
